title: Zechariah 11:1–14
context: The chapter opens with a taunt-like poem: fire devours the cedars of Lebanon, the oaks of Bashan wail, and the shepherds lament because their glory is destroyed. The LORD then commands the prophet to feed the flock of slaughter, whose buyers kill them and whose sellers bless the LORD for their profit. The prophet, acting as shepherd, takes two staffs named Favor and Union, cuts off three shepherds in one month, and gives up the flock. He breaks Favor, annulling a covenant with the peoples, asks for his wages, and is paid thirty pieces of silver, which the LORD tells him to throw to the potter in the LORD’s house. Finally he breaks Union, ending the brotherhood between Judah and Israel. The identities behind the sign-act are much debated. Matthew 26:15 and 27:3-10 take up the thirty pieces of silver, and these notes name those passages without merging them with Zechariah. Historic, typological, and messianic readings of the chapter are held across both traditions, and the notes present them as options rather than as a contrast between the traditions.

verses.text: Open your doors, Lebanon, that the fire may devour your cedars.
verses.arminianNotes: Open your doors, Lebanon, that the fire may devour your cedars. Arminian readers hear a poetic summons announcing judgment, with fire sweeping through the proud forests of the north.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that cedars are often images of rulers or nations elsewhere in the prophets, though the target here is not named. The poem prepares for the shepherd sign-act that follows.

verses.text: Wail, cypress tree, for the cedar has fallen, because the stately ones are destroyed. Wail, you oaks of Bashan, for the strong forest has come down.
verses.arminianNotes: Wail, cypress tree, for the cedar has fallen, Arminian readers see the lament spreading from tree to tree, as the fall of the mighty cedar leaves the lesser trees exposed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the oaks of Bashan join the lament because the strong forest has come down. Whether the trees stand for nations, rulers, or the land itself is debated.

verses.text: A voice of the wailing of the shepherds! For their glory is destroyed—a voice of the roaring of young lions! For the pride of the Jordan is ruined.
verses.arminianNotes: A voice of the wailing of the shepherds! Arminian readers see the leaders lamenting because their glory is destroyed, setting up the theme of failed shepherds in the verses that follow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the parallel image of young lions roaring because the pride of the Jordan is ruined. The thickets along the Jordan were known as lion country, and the image is of a ruined habitat.

verses.text: The LORD my God says: “Feed the flock of slaughter.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD my God says: Arminian readers see the prophet commanded to feed the flock of slaughter, a people already marked for harm by those who should have protected them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the prophet now acts as shepherd in a symbolic action. The command sets the frame for the sign-act, whose details are much debated.

verses.text: Their buyers slaughter them and go unpunished. Those who sell them say, ‘Blessed be the LORD, for I am rich;’ and their own shepherds don’t pity them.
verses.arminianNotes: Their buyers slaughter them and go unpunished. Arminian readers see leaders and traders profiting from the flock’s misery while claiming God’s blessing, saying, Blessed be the LORD, for I am rich.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the flock’s own shepherds don’t pity them. Piety used to cover greed is condemned here, as elsewhere in the prophets (compare Zechariah 10:3).

verses.text: For I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land,” says the LORD; “but, behold, I will deliver every one of the men into his neighbor’s hand and into the hand of his king. They will strike the land, and out of their hand I will not deliver them.”
verses.arminianNotes: For I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land, Arminian readers see the LORD withdrawing his protection, handing people over to their neighbors and their king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the stark statement that the LORD will not deliver them. The Judges 9:23 box treats how the traditions describe God handing people over to hostile powers.

verses.text: So I fed the flock to be slaughtered, especially the oppressed of the flock. I took for myself two staffs. The one I called “Favor” and the other I called “Union”, and I fed the flock.
verses.arminianNotes: So I fed the flock to be slaughtered, especially the oppressed of the flock. Arminian readers see the prophet caring especially for the oppressed of the flock, using two staffs, one called Favor and the other called Union.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the staffs’ names express the LORD’s gracious care and the unity of his people. Their breaking later in the chapter marks the loss of both.

verses.text: I cut off the three shepherds in one month; for my soul was weary of them, and their soul also loathed me.
verses.arminianNotes: I cut off the three shepherds in one month; Arminian readers see judgment on failed leaders, with mutual weariness between the prophet and the flock: my soul was weary of them, and their soul also loathed me.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the identity of the three shepherds is much debated, with many proposals and no agreement. The text gives no names, and the phrase in one month may be literal or a figure for swiftness.

verses.text: Then I said, “I will not feed you. That which dies, let it die; and that which is to be cut off, let it be cut off; and let those who are left eat each other’s flesh.”
verses.arminianNotes: I will not feed you. Arminian readers see the shepherd giving up the flock to its chosen course, a sober picture of judgment after persistent rejection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the grim words that those who are left eat each other’s flesh, read as siege conditions in a land without care. The verse is stark but restrained in detail.

verses.text: I took my staff Favor and cut it apart, that I might break my covenant that I had made with all the peoples.
verses.arminianNotes: I took my staff Favor and cut it apart, Arminian readers see the breaking of the staff as the removal of protection, annulling the covenant the shepherd had made with all the peoples.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the covenant with all the peoples is unclear; some read it as restraint on the nations, others differently. The broken staff signifies the loss of the LORD’s favor.

verses.text: It was broken in that day; and thus the poor of the flock that listened to me knew that it was the LORD’s word.
verses.arminianNotes: It was broken in that day; Arminian readers see the poor of the flock who listened recognizing that the breaking was the LORD’s word, a faithful remnant within a rejecting people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the poor of the flock knew that it was the LORD’s word. Shared ground: both traditions see the humble who listen recognizing God’s hand in judgment.

verses.text: I said to them, “If you think it best, give me my wages; and if not, keep them.” So they weighed for my wages thirty pieces of silver.
verses.arminianNotes: So they weighed for my wages thirty pieces of silver. Arminian readers see the people setting a low value on the shepherd’s service, a sum many compare with the price for a servant in Exodus 21:32.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare Matthew 26:15, where the chief priests weighed out for him thirty pieces of silver. The Matthew 26:15 box treats Judas’s responsibility and God’s purpose; the passages are named without merging.

verses.text: The LORD said to me, “Throw it to the potter—the handsome price that I was valued at by them!” I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them to the potter in the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them to the potter in the LORD’s house. Arminian readers see the LORD’s irony, the handsome price that I was valued at by them, and read Matthew 27:3-10 as fulfillment that leaves human refusal accountable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress God’s sure word governing the price; the Matthew 27:9 and Luke 22:22 boxes treat this. Matthew 27:9 names Jeremiah, and readers point to Jeremiah 18-19 and 32; these notes leave the question open.

verses.text: Then I cut apart my other staff, Union, that I might break the brotherhood between Judah and Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Then I cut apart my other staff, Union, Arminian readers take the cutting of Union as the end of the brotherhood between Judah and Israel, a division following the rejection of the shepherd.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the event in view is debated; compare the joining of two sticks in Ezekiel 37:16-22, which pictures reunion. The two images are named side by side.
